prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence on how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: My laureates are unchanged from round 1 and my first choice is still B018. What I narrowed is the citation, which now rests on the empirical evidence and not on a claim of priority for the task framework. I weigh three things together: new data and credible designs, an explanatory framework, and follow-on work by others. The China-shock papers tie commuting-zone outcomes to import exposure, and the task-based reading of technology explains polarisation and wage inequality. Together they changed how economists and policymakers think about the local, distributional costs of trade and automation. The evidence is transparent and has been re-estimated, challenged and extended by many independent users for more than a decade. I count that as maturity. The round 1 exchange also settled the attribution question I found hardest. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the stable three-name core of the China-shock papers, and Katz's skill demand-and-supply line is a separate, earlier strand that I now treat as context. Nobody in round 1 defended the Katz cut, and Enflo and Strömberg both named the same trio as the stable set. I did not move to B001 because of its first-place count. That count is not evidence of merit and I have not used it as such.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution and framing. The task-based framework has originators outside the credited list (Levy and Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo, Zeira). A citation limited to the trade-shock and labour-demand evidence is cleaner, but it then rewards an empirical-design contribution whose long-run interpretation is debated. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share identification, are still contested. Several colleagues (Andersson, Fredriksson, Hassler, Strömberg, Teorell) think that argues for waiting. A three-name cap also leaves out Katz, whose skill-premium work underlies much of the wider literature. B001's attribution is plainly cleaner than mine, with two names and no identification dispute. I accept that on credit clarity B001 is ahead, and I would be comfortable voting for it if the committee judges clean attribution to outweigh the other criteria.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, ranks B018 fifth. He cites task-framework antecedents (Levy and Murnane) and Acemoglu's related theory, and he says the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trade-shock work is a distinct strand from Katz's skill-premium work. He would not object to B018 later, once persistence evidence settles.
responses.response: I agree with the central part of this. The trade-shock strand and the Katz skill-premium strand are different contributions, and that is why I dropped Katz in round 1 and do not use him as a third name now. I answer the antecedent point by narrowing the citation to evidence on import competition, technological change and local labour markets, with no claim to the task framework. On Acemoglu, I read the 2024 prize as covering institutions and prosperity, so I do not think it covered the task framework. I would still not describe the B018 case as resting on that framework. On waiting, I count a decade of open replication and re-estimation as consolidation. I accept that this is a difference in weighting and not a factual dispute, and your question about whether B018 is one discovery or two is a fair one. My answer is one, if the citation is confined to labour-demand effects of trade and technology shocks.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B018 third and proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues that replacing Dorn with Katz would mix two contributions and omit someone central to the strongest empirical result. She sees B018 as strong but less settled than B001.
responses.response: I agree on the composition, and my round 1 revision reflects it. My opening proposal with Katz does not fit the ballot's own core papers, and I cannot defend it. I do not fully share your view that B018 is less settled than B001. The trade-shock estimates have been tested by many independent users, while the structural protection-for-sale parameters you list as your own main reservation are specification-sensitive. Still, your point about timing is serious and I take it as a real risk to my choice. We agree on the three names, and we differ mainly on how much weight maturity and empirical standing should get against attribution clarity.

responses.point: Strömberg accepts B018's empirical quality and policy relevance. He says the problem is that the credited set is unstable, since my opening named Katz and others named Dorn. He would reconsider if the committee can settle a three-name set and a single stated discovery.
responses.response: That is the condition I have tried to meet. The set is now Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and the stated discovery is how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets. I accept that my opening instability was a real weakness and that it was fair to hold it against B018 at the time. The Levy-Murnane antecedents remain a cost that I cannot remove with wording alone. That is why the citation makes no claim on the task framework. If you reconsidered because the names are now stable, I would want you to weigh the shift-share and persistence debate as an open question and not as a defect.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B018 fourth. He would want the citation confined to the trade-shock strand if the committee goes there. He says the shift-share identification critiques and the long-run persistence question are still being worked through.
responses.response: I have adopted your suggestion on the citation, and it has improved the proposal. Your identification point is the one I find hardest to answer completely. Exposure-design critiques are real, and I would not say they are resolved. My view is that they have been addressed openly by the authors and their critics, with new work on exposure designs and on persistence, and that this is how a mature empirical contribution behaves. You and I are close on importance, and we disagree on whether an open identification debate argues for waiting. I do not see a design-based case for waiting when the evidence is this transparent and has been replicated and re-estimated so widely.

responses.point: Krusell says B001 is cleaner on attribution, and he is more concerned than the supporters about mixed empirical support for protection-for-sale. He says a prize built on the trade-shock strand alone with Autor, Dorn and Hanson might be defensible, but that a prize crediting the task framework is harder to cite.
responses.response: I agree that the trade-shock-only citation is the defensible one, and that is the version I propose. Your concern about the empirical record of protection-for-sale also bears on the chair's question about B001. I have not moved B001 to first because a theoretical framework with mixed test results is harder for me to weigh than evidence that has been replicated. But I do not treat that as disqualifying, and the B001 supporters make a serious case that a testable framework deserves credit even where estimates are fragile. I keep B001 as an alternative on those grounds.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the trade-shock and technology evidence as one coherent discovery or as two strands that need separate citations.
How far the long-run persistence and magnitude of trade-shock effects will survive continued re-estimation, and whether shift-share identification critiques will change the interpretation.
Whether mixed empirical support for protection-for-sale (B001) should count as a disqualifying limit or as a normal feature of a productive framework. I treat it as a real but not decisive limit.
How to handle task-framework originators who are not credited on B018 (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo) without implying priority for the credited names.
My statements about earlier prizes, the 2024 and 2025 awards and external literatures are taken from colleagues' files and general knowledge, and I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot, and I have no documented tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Grossman, Helpman, Kiyotaki or Moore. I work in labour economics, so B018 is close to my own field. I disclose that as field proximity, not as a personal connection, and I have tried to apply the same criteria across fields. I have read the other members' disclosures and do not adjudicate them.
